# Shared schedule shows Fenwick which repairs await parts

After a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule, Fenwick Instrument Repairs approved it for new jobs but held back its backlog. The account shows that agreeing what each status meant was the workshop's work, not the software's.

By Thomas Barregren

Fenwick Instrument Repairs services brass and woodwind instruments. Before the trial, jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work appeared on separate paper sheets. In January 2026 the workshop team began six weeks with a shared schedule, choosing Benchline after checking that it could tell those statuses apart. Its manager, Priya Vale, describes what had to be settled and what would be done differently.

## The workshop set the statuses, Benchline configured them

Asked in an email interview what the team had to settle before the schedule was useful, Vale replied: 'We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.'

The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session. Collection arrangements stayed on the telephone, where the team continued to discuss them with customers.

## Trial summary leaves repair speed unmeasured

The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts. It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.

What the trial established, then, is the team's reported experience rather than a measured improvement in repair speed. Vale approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.

## Vale would check the definitions for longer next time

Would Vale make the same choice again? 'I would use it again for new jobs,' Vale wrote. 'I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.'

For a workshop considering a shared schedule, Fenwick's account suggests where to spend time first: agreeing what each status means, and who updates it, before any backlog goes in.
EOF

# Shared schedule shows Fenwick which repairs await parts

After a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule, Fenwick Instrument Repairs approved it for new jobs but held back its backlog. The account shows that agreeing what each status meant was the workshop's work, not the software's.

By Thomas Barregren

Fenwick Instrument Repairs services brass and woodwind instruments. Before the trial, jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work appeared on separate paper sheets. In January 2026 the workshop team began six weeks with a shared schedule, choosing Benchline after checking that it could tell those statuses apart. Its manager, Priya Vale, describes what had to be settled and what would be done differently.

## The workshop set the statuses, Benchline configured them

Asked in an email interview what the team had to settle before the schedule was useful, Vale replied: 'We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.'

The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session. Collection arrangements stayed on the telephone, where the team continued to discuss them with customers.

## Trial summary leaves repair speed unmeasured

The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts. It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.

What the trial established, then, is the team's reported experience rather than a measured improvement in repair speed. Vale approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.

## Vale would check the definitions for longer next time

Would Vale make the same choice again? 'I would use it again for new jobs,' Vale wrote. 'I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.'

For a workshop considering a shared schedule, Fenwick's account suggests where to spend time first: agreeing what each status means, and who updates it, before any backlog goes in.
EOF

# Source-comparison report: draft2.md

Draft: /private/var/folders/cs/vgp_x_353zd9frkjpysp7zdw0000gn/T/kntnt-editorial-388-run-3b6vzwwx/scratch/write-sc.hpz6jG/draft2.md
Source: /private/var/folders/cs/vgp_x_353zd9frkjpysp7zdw0000gn/T/kntnt-editorial-388-run-3b6vzwwx/work/source.md
Language: draft in British English (en_GB); material in English. No translation is involved, so there are no translation findings. All quotations are checked verbatim against the English material.

## 1. Claim accounting

Each row gives the draft passage, the source passage in the material's words, and what differs.

**C1. Title (l.1).** "Fenwick says staff could see repairs awaiting parts"
Source: "The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, ... It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts."
Difference: "Fenwick says" covers "the workshop's trial summary", which is Fenwick's own document, so the attribution holds. "Repairs awaiting parts" and "instruments ... waiting for parts" name the same jobs; the material treats the jobs as repairs ("repair duration"). "Could" keeps the past tense and the trial context. **Supported.**

**C2. Standfirst, sentence 1 (l.3).** "After trialling a shared bench schedule, Fenwick Instrument Repairs' manager approved it for new jobs but held back the backlog."
Source: "In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule." / "The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions."
Differences:
(a) "Held back" is not the same as "postponed ... until the team had reviewed its status definitions". The temporary nature and its condition are lost. See F1.
(b) "After trialling" puts the approval after the trial. The material does not date the approval. See F2.
(c) "The manager" is Vale. The brief's singular "its manager" and the material's "workshop manager Priya Vale" settle this. Supported.

**C3. Standfirst, sentence 2 (l.3).** "The account makes clear that agreeing what each status meant was the workshop's work, not the software's."
Source: "The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices"; Vale: "We had to agree what ready for work meant."
Difference: "Agreeing what each status meant" corresponds to "defined the statuses". "Not the software's" corresponds to Benchline configuring "those choices", meaning the workshop's choices. "The account" reads in context as the case as told, which is the material. It does not put words into Vale's mouth. "Makes clear" is warranted because the material states the division directly. **Supported.**

**C4. Byline (l.5).** "By Thomas Barregren". This comes from the invocation. Per the instructions, it is not a finding.

**C5. (l.7)** "Fenwick Instrument Repairs services brass and woodwind instruments."
Source: identical sentence. **Supported.**

**C6. (l.7)** "Before the trial, jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work appeared on separate paper sheets."
Source: "Previously, jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work appeared on separate paper sheets."
Difference: the source's "previously" follows the sentence about the trial starting, so it means before the trial. **Supported.**

**C7. (l.7)** "In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule, having chosen Benchline after checking that it could tell those statuses apart."
Source: "In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule." / "The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish these statuses."
Differences: "tell apart" and "distinguish" mean the same, and "it" means Benchline in both. The perfect participle "having chosen" says the choice came before the trial began. The material gives no order for the two events. See F3.

**C8. (l.7)** "The workshop's manager, Priya Vale, describes what had to be settled and what would be done differently."
Source: "workshop manager Priya Vale"; Q: "What did the team have to settle ...?"; Q: "... what would you change?" Vale: "I would allow another week ..."
Difference: "What would be done differently" stays conditional, matching Vale's hypothetical "I would". The brief also asks for "what its manager would approach differently". **Supported.**

**C9. Heading (l.9).** "The workshop set the statuses, Benchline configured them"
Source: "The workshop defined the statuses ... Benchline configured those choices".
Difference: "configured them" (the statuses) against "configured those choices" (the definitions and who updates them). No case separates the two. **Supported.**

**C10. (l.11)** "Asked in an email interview what the team had to settle before the schedule was useful, Vale replied: 'We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.'"
Source: "email interview on 2 March 2026"; Q: "What did the team have to settle before the schedule was useful?"; Vale: "We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench."
Difference: the quotation is verbatim, keeping the hedge "did not always". The question is paraphrased faithfully. "Replied" fits an email exchange, and nothing spoken is implied. Publication is approved per the material, and the draft makes no claim about approval. **Supported.**

**C11. (l.13)** "The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session. The team continued to use telephone calls to discuss collection arrangements with customers."
Source: identical sentences. **Supported.**

**C12. Heading (l.15).** "Trial summary leaves repair speed unmeasured"
Source: "It does not measure repair duration ..." and "not a measured improvement in repair speed".
Difference: the heading limits the claim to the summary, and "speed" corresponds to "duration". **Supported.**

**C13. (l.17)** Trial summary dated 23 February 2026, 38 jobs, staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts, and no measurement of repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.
Source: identical sentences. **Supported.**

**C14. (l.19)** "What the summary and interview establish, then, is the team's reported experience rather than a measured improvement in repair speed."
Source: "The summary and interview establish the team's reported experience, not a measured improvement in repair speed or a recommendation for every workshop."
Difference: "then" is a transition. Dropping "or a recommendation for every workshop" narrows the sentence but does not change it. **Supported.** (See E1 on the closing paragraph.)

**C15. (l.19)** "Vale approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions."
Source: "The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions."
Difference: "The manager" becomes "Vale", which C2(c) settles. The condition and the time order are kept. **Supported.**

**C16. Heading (l.21).** "Vale would spend longer checking the status names"
Source: Vale: "I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog."
Difference: "spend longer" drops the amount ("another week") and the scope ("before adding the backlog"), but it does not change the claim. Allowing another week to check means a longer period of checking, so neither statement can hold while the other fails. The conditional "would" is kept. **Supported.**

**C17. (l.23)** "Would Vale make the same choice again? 'I would use it again for new jobs,' Vale wrote. 'I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.'"
Source: Q: "Would you make the same choice again, and what would you change?" Vale: "I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog."
Difference: both sentences are verbatim, split by an attribution. "Wrote" is correct for email. Vale's "for new jobs" limit survives beside the draft's broader question. **Supported.**

**C18. (l.25)** "A workshop weighing a shared schedule of its own could start where Fenwick had to: by agreeing what each status means, and checking the names, before any backlog goes in."
Source: Vale: "We had to agree what ready for work meant."; "The manager ... postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions."; Vale: "I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog."; and "not ... a recommendation for every workshop."
Difference: the advice itself is the author's own advocacy, softened by "could". But it presents as fact that Fenwick "had to" start by checking the names before the backlog went in. The material presents that step as a decision and a hindsight preference, not a necessity, and it came after the trial, not at the start. See F4. On the advice's scope, see E1.

### Pronoun accounting

- l.3 "approved it": third person, singular, neuter. The referent is the shared bench schedule, matching the source's "continued use" of it. No natural-gender content.
- l.7 "it could tell those statuses apart": third person, singular, neuter. The referent is Benchline, as in the source's "it could distinguish". "Those" is plural and refers to "awaiting parts" and "ready for work", as in the source's "these statuses".
- l.17 "It says" / "It does not": third person, singular, neuter. The referent is the trial summary, as in the source.
- l.19 "its status definitions": third person, singular, neuter. The referent is the team, as in the source.
- l.25 "its own": third person, singular. The referent is the hypothetical workshop. This is the author's generic phrasing.
- In the quotations, "We", "I" and "it" are verbatim from Vale. First person plural "we" is the team and first person singular "I" is Vale, as in the source.
- The draft uses no gendered pronoun for Vale and makes no natural-gender assertion. The material gives none either. English has no grammatical gender at issue here.

## 2. Findings (source support)

**F1. Standfirst (l.3): "held back the backlog" loses the postponement and its condition.** PLAUSIBLE, low severity.
- Draft: "approved it for new jobs but held back the backlog."
- Source: "postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions."
- Two-way test: suppose the manager decided never to add the backlog. "Held back" (withheld) would still be true, but "postponed ... until" would be false. So the draft allows a reading, an open-ended or permanent withholding, that the material does not support. The summary is where the contract requires qualifications to be kept. The body (l.19) restores the condition, but the standfirst does not.
- Smallest repair: "... approved it for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog." Optionally keep the condition: "... until the team had reviewed its status definitions."

**F2. Standfirst (l.3): "After trialling" puts the approval after the trial without support.** PLAUSIBLE, low severity.
- Draft: "After trialling a shared bench schedule, Fenwick Instrument Repairs' manager approved it ..."
- Source: "In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial ..."; "The manager approved continued use for new jobs ..." The approval is not dated.
- Two-way test: suppose the trial began on 26 January 2026, which fits "In January 2026", so its six weeks ran to about 9 March. The manager then approved continued use on or around the 23 February summary, before the trial ended. The material says the approval followed some use ("continued use"), but the draft, read as "after the trial", fails. No supplied statement dates the approval or the end of the trial.
- Smallest repair, combined with F1: "Fenwick Instrument Repairs trialled a shared bench schedule; its manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog."

**F3. (l.7): "having chosen Benchline" says the choice came before the trial began.** PLAUSIBLE, low severity.
- Draft: "In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule, having chosen Benchline after checking that it could tell those statuses apart."
- Source: "In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule." / "The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish these statuses." The two sentences are separate, and their order is not stated.
- Two-way test: suppose the team started the shared schedule in early January on an interim sheet, then checked Benchline and chose it in the second week. The material holds, but "having chosen" (the choice before the trial began) fails. No supplied statement dates the choice.
- Smallest repair: split the sentence the way the source does. "In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule. The team chose Benchline after checking that it could tell those statuses apart."

**F4. Closing (l.25): "where Fenwick had to" turns a decision and a hindsight preference into a necessity, and places it at Fenwick's start.** CONFIRMED, moderate severity.
- Draft: "could start where Fenwick had to: by agreeing what each status means, and checking the names, before any backlog goes in."
- Source: necessity is stated only for "We had to agree what ready for work meant", and only "before the schedule was useful". The backlog step is a decision: "The manager ... postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions". Vale's extra checking time is a hindsight preference: "I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog."
- Two-way test: the material is consistent with the backlog review having been the manager's cautious choice, not a requirement. In that case the draft's "Fenwick had to ... check the names before any backlog goes in" is false while every source statement holds. The review also followed the trial, so it was not where Fenwick "started". No supplied statement makes the review of names necessary.
- Smallest repair: "could begin where Fenwick had to, by agreeing what each status means, and, as Vale would now, allow time to check the names before any backlog goes in."

## 3. Editorial question (not a defect)

**E1. Closing advice (l.25) against the material's disclaimer.** The material says the summary and interview do not establish "a recommendation for every workshop", and the brief says "No ... call to action is supplied." The closing sentence is the author's own advice about process. It is hedged ("could") and does not recommend Benchline, and it is not attributed to Fenwick or Vale. So it is defensible as the author's advocacy based on supported material. Whether the publisher wants any general advice in a case the material explicitly keeps from generalising is an editorial decision, not a source-support defect. The facts in the passage are covered by F4.

## 4. Translation findings

None. The draft and the material are both in English, and every quotation is verbatim.

## Completion status

Complete. Every factual and attributed claim in the title, standfirst, headings, body and closing has been accounted for, including pronouns. Four source-support findings are unresolved in the draft: F1, F2 and F3 (low severity, PLAUSIBLE) and F4 (moderate severity, CONFIRMED). One editorial question, E1, is open. There are no translation findings.

## 3. Findings (source support)

**F1. Title turns the summary's report into an unattributed present-tense fact**
- Draft: "Shared schedule shows Fenwick which repairs await parts"
- Source: "It [the workshop's trial summary] says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts." / "The summary and interview establish the team's reported experience".
- Difference: whose assertion (the summary says it, versus the draft asserting it), and time (past trial report, versus the general present).
- Case: the summary reports that staff could see this, but some jobs were not accurately placed. Vale's own remark allows for that: "A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench", and the manager postponed the backlog "until the team had reviewed its status definitions". Here the source statement holds and the title's unqualified fact fails. Nothing in the material rules this case out.
- Smallest repair: "Shared schedule let Fenwick staff see which repairs awaited parts, trial summary says". Any equivalent that keeps both the attribution and the past tense also works.

**F2. Standfirst: chronology of the approval, and who approved**
- Draft: "After a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule, Fenwick Instrument Repairs approved it for new jobs"
- Source: "In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial" / "The manager approved continued use for new jobs".
- Difference: the source gives no date for the approval and does not say that the trial ran its full six weeks before the approval. The summary is dated 23 February. A trial begun after 12 January would not have completed six weeks by then. Separately, the source says the manager approved, not the firm.
- Case: the trial began on 26 January (six weeks would end on 9 March), and the manager approved continued use while it was still running. "Continued use" implies only that there had been some use before. Nothing in the material rules this case out.
- Smallest repair: "After trialling a shared bench schedule, Fenwick Instrument Repairs' manager approved it for new jobs but held back the backlog." The six-week length stays in the body as the length of the trial they began.

**F3. "Working from" replaces "a trial of"**
- Draft: "began six weeks of working from a shared schedule"
- Source: "began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule".
- Difference: manner. "Working from" asserts that the schedule was the team's working basis. The source says only that they trialled it.
- Case: during the trial, staff entered jobs into the schedule (38 were recorded) while still working from the paper sheets. The source statement holds and the draft's fails. Nothing in the material says the paper sheets were dropped.
- Smallest repair: "In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule, having chosen Benchline …".

**F4. "Its manager" can be read as Benchline's manager**
- Draft: "…having chosen Benchline after checking that it could tell those statuses apart. Its manager, Priya Vale, describes…"
- Source: "workshop manager Priya Vale".
- Difference: the subject. The nearest earlier "it" refers to Benchline, so "Its manager" can attach to the supplier. That would make Vale Benchline's manager, which the material contradicts.

- Draft: "Collection arrangements stayed on the telephone, where the team continued to discuss them with customers."
- Source: "The team continued to use telephone calls to discuss collection arrangements with customers."
- Difference: scope. The draft says the arrangements themselves stayed off the schedule. The source says only that phone discussion continued.

- Smallest repair: "The team continued to use telephone calls to discuss collection arrangements with customers."

**F6. "What the trial established" replaces "The summary and interview establish"**
- Draft: "What the trial established, then, is the team's reported experience rather than a measured improvement in repair speed."
- Source: "The summary and interview establish the team's reported experience, not a measured improvement in repair speed or a recommendation for every workshop."
- Difference: the subject and the state of knowledge. The source limits what these two documents establish. The draft says the trial itself established no measured improvement. The interview (2 March) is also not part of the trial.
- Case: the workshop's own job records from the trial, which are not in the summary, contain timing data. The source statement holds, and the draft's "the trial established … rather than a measured improvement" fails. The material says only that the summary "does not measure repair duration".
- Smallest repair: "What the summary and interview establish, then, is the team's reported experience rather than a measured improvement in repair speed."

**F7. Heading: "definitions" replaces Vale's "status names"**
- Draft: "Vale would check the definitions for longer next time"
- Source (Vale): "I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog."
- Difference: the thing named. Vale spoke of the status names. "Status definitions" appears only in the narrator's account of the manager's postponement.
- Case: Vale would use the extra week to check the names (labels) of already agreed statuses, not to reopen their definitions. Her statement holds and the heading fails. Nothing in the material rules this case out.
- Smallest repair: "Vale would check the status names for longer next time".

**F8. Closing paragraph attributes to Fenwick's account a lesson for other workshops and adds "who updates it"**
- Draft: "For a workshop considering a shared schedule, Fenwick's account suggests where to spend time first: agreeing what each status means, and who updates it, before any backlog goes in."

- Case: at Fenwick, deciding who would update the statuses was quick and took no significant time. The source holds, and the draft's attributed suggestion fails.

For example: "Fenwick's account is one team's reported experience: agreeing what the statuses meant had to come before the schedule was useful, and Vale would allow another week to check the status names before any backlog goes in."
